Old vs New Tax Regime India (FY 2026-27): Which is Better for You?

📌 Key Takeaways

  • New Regime is now the default for salaried individuals since FY 2023-24.
  • Income up to ₹12.75 lakh is effectively tax-free in the New Regime (with standard deduction).
  • Old Regime is beneficial only if your total deductions exceed ₹3.75 lakh.
  • Salaried employees can switch regimes every year at the time of filing ITR.

Every April, the same question haunts millions of salaried Indians: Should I stick with the Old Tax Regime or switch to the New one? The Finance Act 2026 brings updated slabs but no dramatic restructuring, making this decision more important than ever.

This guide cuts through the noise with a clear slab-by-slab comparison, real salary examples, and a simple decision rule so you can make the right call in minutes — not hours.

Standard Deduction: Both regimes allow a standard deduction of ₹75,000 for salaried employees from FY 2024-25 onwards. This means your New Regime taxable income starts from ₹75,000 below your gross salary.

What Deductions Are Available in Each Regime?

📌 Old Tax Regime

  • Standard Deduction: ₹50,000
  • Section 80C: up to ₹1.5 lakh (PPF, ELSS, EPF, LIC)
  • Section 80D: Health insurance premium
  • HRA Exemption
  • LTA (Leave Travel Allowance)
  • Home Loan Interest (Section 24b): up to ₹2 lakh
  • Section 80CCD(1B): NPS ₹50,000
  • Section 80TTA: Savings interest ₹10,000
  • Education Loan Interest (80E)

📌 New Tax Regime

  • Standard Deduction: ₹75,000 ✔
  • Section 80CCD(2): Employer NPS contribution ✔
  • Agniveer Corpus Fund ✔
  • 80C: Not available ✘
  • HRA: Not available ✘
  • Home Loan Interest: Not available ✘
  • 80D (Health Insurance): Not available ✘
  • LTA: Not available ✘

The Break-Even Point: When Old Regime Makes Sense

The Old Regime becomes beneficial when your total eligible deductions exceed the "break-even" threshold compared to the New Regime's lower slabs. For most salary levels, this threshold sits around ₹3.5–4.5 lakh in deductions.

Salary Min. Deductions for Old Regime to Win
₹10 lakh~ ₹3.0 lakh
₹15 lakh~ ₹3.75 lakh
₹20 lakh~ ₹4.25 lakh
₹25 lakh~ ₹4.75 lakh
₹30 lakh+~ ₹5.5 lakh

Which Regime Should You Choose? A Simple Decision Guide

Answer these questions in order:

  1. Is your gross salary below ₹12.75 lakh?
    → New Regime — you pay zero tax. Stop here.
  2. Do you pay rent and claim HRA?
    Add your annual HRA exemption amount.
  3. Do you invest ₹1.5 lakh in 80C instruments? (PPF, ELSS, EPF, LIC, etc.)
    Add ₹1.5 lakh.
  4. Do you have a home loan?
    Add up to ₹2 lakh of interest paid.
  5. Do you pay health insurance premiums? (80D)
    Add up to ₹50,000.
  6. Total your deductions.
    If total > break-even for your salary (see table above) → Old Regime
    If total < break-even → New Regime

What About Senior Citizens & Super Seniors?

Senior citizens (60–80 years) get a basic exemption of ₹3 lakh under the Old Regime, and super senior citizens (above 80 years) get ₹5 lakh. These higher exemptions can tip the balance towards the Old Regime for retirees with fixed deposits and insurance deductions. The New Regime does not offer age-based exemption differences.

Can You Switch Every Year?

Salaried individuals without business income can switch between the Old and New Tax Regime every financial year, simply by indicating their choice at the time of filing the ITR or submitting Form 12BB to their employer. This flexibility is significant — you can optimise year-by-year based on actual investments made.

However, individuals with income from business or profession can switch from New to Old only once. After switching back to Old, they cannot return to New.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the key differences between the Old and New Tax Regimes in India?

The Old Regime offers extensive deductions (80C, HRA, home loan interest, 80D) but higher tax rates for mid-income earners. The New Regime has lower, simplified slabs — especially between ₹5–12 lakh — but removes most deductions. The net effect depends on how much you can legitimately claim in deductions.

Is income up to ₹12 lakh really tax-free in FY 2026-27?

Yes, for salaried individuals in the New Regime. The Section 87A rebate makes taxable income up to ₹12 lakh effectively tax-free, and the ₹75,000 standard deduction means a gross salary of ₹12.75 lakh results in zero tax. Note: this rebate is not available if you have special-rate income (e.g. LTCG from equity).

What are the tax slabs for the New Regime in FY 2026-27?

New Regime slabs: Nil up to ₹4L, 5% (₹4L–8L), 10% (₹8L–12L), 15% (₹12L–16L), 20% (₹16L–20L), 25% (₹20L–24L), 30% above ₹24L. Standard deduction of ₹75,000 also applies for salaried employees, reducing your taxable income by that amount.

Can I switch between Old and New Tax Regime every year?

Salaried individuals (without business income) can switch regimes freely every financial year. You simply declare your preferred regime to your employer via Form 12BB and confirm it when filing your ITR. Individuals with business income can switch from New to Old only once.

What deductions are allowed in the New Tax Regime?

The New Regime allows standard deduction (₹75,000), employer NPS contribution under Section 80CCD(2), and Agniveer Corpus Fund deduction. Most other deductions — 80C, HRA, LTA, home loan interest under 24b, 80D health insurance, 80TTA — are not available.

How do I calculate which regime is better for my salary?

Calculate your total deductions (standard deduction + 80C + HRA + home loan interest + 80D + NPS). Compare your tax in both regimes. If the total deduction amount exceeds the break-even threshold for your salary (see the table in this article), the Old Regime saves you more.
